result:
**Marginalia**

There's a particular pleasure in finding evidence of a stranger's life inside a used book. A cinema ticket from 1987, folded twice. A grocery list in loopy cursive: milk, bread, something energetically crossed out. A flower pressed so long it has become tissue paper, its color surrendered entirely to time.

These fragments turn reading into archaeology. Someone loved this book before you did—or at least carried it, forgot it, used it as a coaster during a difficult summer. The water ring on the cover is a small confession.

My favorite finds are the marginalia. A neat *yes* in the margin of a philosophy text. An angry slash through a poem stanza, as if the reader took it personally. Once, in a used copy of *Middlemarch*, I found a phone number and the words "call her, you coward." I have spent years wondering whether he did.

Books are supposed to be about the words, but they're also objects that live alongside us. They absorb our lives the way wood absorbs the smell of a kitchen. A paperback swollen from being read in the bath. A spine cracked at the same scene, over and over, because someone only ever needed that one page.

When I buy used books, I inherit all of this. The previous reader becomes a ghost companion, someone whose taste I can reconstruct from dog-ears and underlines. We never met, but we sat with the same sentences, and they left their fingerprints on the pages for me to find, decades later, in a shop that smells of dust and glue and other people's winters.
